cues.text: A Basque Nobleman at Paris

Born in 1506 at the family castle of Xavier in the Kingdom of Navarre, Francisco de Jasso y Xavier came from minor Basque nobility whose fortunes had been battered by Navarre's conquest during his childhood.
Sent to study at the University of Paris at nineteen, the ambitious, athletic young Francis was more interested in academic honors than religious vocation.
At the Collège de Sainte-Barbe he shared a room with an older, deeply serious Basque soldier-turned-pilgrim, Ignatius of Loyola , who had already undergone his own dramatic conversion.
Ignatius pursued Francis patiently for years, repeatedly challenging him with the Gospel question, "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?"
The persistence eventually broke through Xavier's ambition.
Founding the Society of Jesus

On 15 August 1534 , Francis joined Ignatius and five other companions at Montmartre, vowing poverty, chastity, and a pilgrimage to the Holy Land — the founding act of what would become the Society of Jesus .
Political turmoil made the Jerusalem pilgrimage impossible, and the small band instead placed themselves at the pope's disposal.
Ordained a priest in Venice in 1537, Francis worked in Italy for several years until King John III of Portugal, seeking missionaries for his Asian territories, requested two Jesuits from Ignatius.
When one of the chosen men fell ill, Ignatius asked Francis to go in his place.
Francis reportedly packed within a day, saying only, "I am ready."
India and the Malay Archipelago
Xavier reached Goa , the center of Portuguese India, in May 1542 after a grueling thirteen-month voyage.
He threw himself into work among the pearl fishers of the southern Indian coast, the Paravas.
He taught children by walking through villages, ringing a bell, and gathering them to learn the catechism set to simple melodies, since he had not yet mastered their language well enough to preach.
Over the following years he pushed steadily further east — to Malacca, the Moluccas, and remote island communities — enduring shipwreck, tropical disease, and hostile rulers.
By later estimates, he converted tens of thousands, though later historians have debated the pace and permanence of these mass conversions, given how briefly he could remain in any one place.
The Mission to Japan
In Malacca in 1547, Xavier met a Japanese fugitive named Anjiro , whose account of his homeland convinced Xavier that Japan represented fertile, unreached ground.
Xavier sailed for Japan in 1549 with Anjiro as interpreter and two Jesuit companions, landing at Kagoshima.
There, he began a mission remarkable for its cultural adaptation: Xavier studied Japanese customs carefully and adopted more formal dress to gain the respect of the samurai class.
He sought audiences with local lords rather than preaching indiscriminately in the streets as he had in India.
The Japanese mission, though difficult and slow, took root and would grow into one of the most vibrant, and later most persecuted, Christian communities in Asia.
Death Within Sight of China

Convinced that converting Japan fully required first reaching China , then the intellectual and cultural wellspring of East Asia, Xavier resolved to enter the closed empire by whatever means necessary.
He reached the small island of Sancian off the Chinese coast in 1552, arranging with a merchant to be smuggled onto the mainland.
Before the arrangement could be carried out, Xavier fell seriously ill in a makeshift hut on the island.
He died there on 3 December 1552 , alone but for a young Chinese Christian companion, having never set foot on the mainland he had crossed the world to reach.
Legacy
Xavier's body, reportedly found remarkably well preserved months after burial, was eventually enshrined at the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa.
It remains one of the most visited Christian relics in Asia; his right forearm, the hand that had baptized so many converts, was later severed and sent to the Jesuit mother church in Rome.
Canonized alongside Ignatius in 1622, he was declared patron of all foreign missions in 1927.

Regarded by the Church as the greatest missionary since the Apostle Paul, Xavier's decade in Asia established patterns — linguistic study, cultural adaptation, training of native clergy — that would shape Catholic missionary method for centuries after him.
